courses.title: Forensic Science: Principles and Criminology, BSc Semester 1

topics.title: History, principles and branches
topics.summary: Definition, history, basic principles and branches of forensic science.
notes: Forensic science applies scientific methods to questions of law.
Locard's exchange principle: every contact leaves a trace.
Other principles: individuality, progressive change, comparison, analysis, probability.
Pioneers: Bertillon (anthropometry), Galton and Henry (fingerprints), Locard (first police crime laboratory, Lyon, 1910).
Branches: biology, serology, DNA, chemistry, toxicology, physics, ballistics, documents, fingerprints, digital forensics.
outcomes: State and apply Locard's exchange principle
Name the branches of forensic science and their work

lesson.hook: A burglar wears gloves and wipes the door handle. What might he still leave behind, and take away?

questions.q: Who established the first police crime laboratory?
What does the principle of individuality say?
questions.a: Every object, natural or man-made, has an individuality that is not duplicated in another object.

topics.title: Forensic laboratories in India
topics.summary: Organisation of forensic science services in India.
notes: Central Forensic Science Laboratories (CFSLs) work under the Directorate of Forensic Science Services (DFSS), Ministry of Home Affairs.
Each state has a State FSL with Regional and District mobile units.
Other agencies: Central Fingerprint Bureau (NCRB), Government Examiners of Questioned Documents, National Forensic Sciences University (Gandhinagar).
BNSS section 176(3) requires a forensic expert to visit the crime scene for offences punishable with seven years or more.
outcomes: Describe the structure of forensic services in India
Explain the mandatory forensic visit under BNSS

topics.title: Crime and its causes
topics.summary: Concepts of crime, schools of criminology and theories of causation.
notes: Crime is an act or omission punishable by law; criminology studies crime, criminals and society's response.
Schools: classical (Beccaria, free will and deterrence), positivist (Lombroso, born criminal), sociological.
Theories: differential association (Sutherland), strain (Merton), labelling, routine activity.
outcomes: Apply theories to explain a crime

topics.title: Expert evidence
topics.summary: Admissibility of scientific evidence and the role of the expert witness.
notes: BSA section 39 (formerly Evidence Act section 45) makes the opinion of experts relevant.
Reports of certain government scientific experts can be used as evidence without calling them (BNSS section 329).
An expert must be qualified, impartial, and explain the basis of the opinion; the court decides the weight.
Chain of custody documents every transfer of evidence.
outcomes: Explain the role and duties of an expert witness

courses.title: Crime Scene Investigation and Fingerprints, BSc Semester 2

topics.title: Securing and searching a crime scene
topics.summary: First responder duties, scene protection and search methods.
notes: First responder: ensure safety, give aid, secure and cordon the scene, record entry and exit.
Search patterns: spiral, strip (line), grid, zone, wheel (ray).
Indoor scenes favour zone searches; large outdoor scenes favour grid or line searches.

topics.title: Notes, photography and sketching
topics.summary: Recording the crime scene before evidence is moved.
notes: Photography: overall, mid-range and close-up (with and without a scale).
Sketches: rough sketch at the scene, finished sketch later; measurements by triangulation or baseline.
Notes record date, time, weather, people present and observations.
outcomes: Document a scene by photographs and sketches

topics.title: Packaging and preservation
topics.summary: Collecting, packaging and preserving physical and biological evidence.
notes: Biological evidence is air-dried and packed in paper (not plastic) to prevent mould.
Volatile samples (arson debris) go in airtight metal cans.
Each item is sealed, labelled and recorded in the chain of custody.
outcomes: Choose packaging for each evidence type

topics.title: Fingerprint patterns and classification
topics.summary: Ridge characteristics, pattern types and the Henry system.
notes: Fingerprints are unique and permanent from fetal life.
Pattern types: arches (about 5%), loops (60–65%), whorls (30–35%).
A loop has one delta; a whorl two; a plain arch none.
Henry classification assigns values to whorls in finger pairs to form a primary classification.
outcomes: Identify arch, loop and whorl patterns

resources.title: Fingerprint patterns: arch, loop and whorl

lesson.hook: Identical twins share the same DNA. Do they share fingerprints?

questions.q: Which pattern type is the most common?
How many deltas does a whorl have?

topics.title: Developing and comparing latent prints
topics.summary: Powder, chemical and physical methods, and minutiae comparison.
notes: Powder dusting on smooth non-porous surfaces; ninhydrin on paper (reacts with amino acids, purple colour).
Cyanoacrylate fuming develops prints on non-porous items; iodine fuming is non-destructive and temporary.
Comparison uses minutiae (ridge endings, bifurcations, dots, islands); ACE-V method: analysis, comparison, evaluation, verification.
outcomes: Choose a development method for a surface

resources.title: Matching a chance print by minutiae

courses.title: Questioned Documents and Forensic Physics, BSc Semester 3

topics.title: Handwriting and signature examination
topics.summary: Principles of handwriting identification and forgery.
notes: No two people write alike, and no one writes exactly the same way twice (natural variation).
Class characteristics (taught system) vs individual characteristics (habits).
Forgery types: simulated, traced, freehand; signs include tremor, pen lifts, blunt starts and patching.
Admitted and specimen writings are standards for comparison.

topics.title: Inks, alterations and paper
topics.summary: Detecting alterations, erasures and ink differences.
notes: Alterations show under UV, IR and oblique light; VSC (video spectral comparator) is the standard instrument.
Inks are compared by thin-layer chromatography.
Indentations are revealed by ESDA (electrostatic detection apparatus).

topics.title: Glass and soil evidence
topics.summary: Physical properties used to compare glass and soil.
notes: Glass is compared by density and refractive index (immersion method, Becke line).
Radial cracks form on the side opposite the impact; concentric cracks on the same side (3R rule: radial cracks form right angles on the reverse side).
Soil is compared by colour, particle size and mineral content.
outcomes: Compare glass fragments by density and RI
Determine direction of force from fracture lines

resources.title: Refractive index of glass by the Becke line

topics.title: Tool marks and impressions
topics.summary: Footwear, tyre and tool mark evidence.
notes: Impressions may be 2-D (dust, blood) or 3-D (mud, snow); 3-D impressions are cast with dental stone.
Class characteristics (sole pattern, size) narrow the source; wear and damage individualise it.
Stature can be estimated from foot length using population-specific regression formulae.

topics.title: Firearms and ballistics
topics.summary: Firearm classification, internal, external and terminal ballistics.
notes: Rifled arms leave land and groove marks on bullets; smooth-bore (shotguns) do not.
Internal ballistics: inside the barrel; external: in flight; terminal: on the target.
Entry wounds are smaller with abrasion collars; exit wounds are larger and irregular.
Range of fire is estimated from soot and tattooing (powder stippling).

courses.title: Forensic Chemistry and Toxicology, BSc Semester 4

topics.title: Narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances
topics.summary: Classification of drugs, the NDPS Act and presumptive tests.
notes: NDPS Act, 1985 controls narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances; quantities are classed small, intermediate or commercial.
Classes: opioids (morphine, heroin), stimulants (cocaine, amphetamines), depressants, hallucinogens (LSD), cannabinoids.
Presumptive colour tests: Marquis (opiates, amphetamines), Duquenois–Levine (cannabis), cobalt thiocyanate (cocaine).
Confirmation needs instrumental methods such as GC-MS.

topics.title: Poisons and their analysis
topics.summary: Classification of poisons, specimens and extraction.
notes: Paracelsus: "the dose makes the poison".
Classes: corrosives, irritants (metallic: arsenic, mercury, lead), neurotoxins, asphyxiants (CO, cyanide).
Viscera (stomach, intestine, liver, kidney), blood and urine are preserved; saturated salt solution is used for viscera (not in cases of corrosive acid poisoning).
Stas–Otto method extracts alkaloids and organic poisons.

topics.title: Arson and explosives
topics.summary: Fire chemistry, accelerants and explosive residues.
notes: Fire triangle: fuel, heat, oxygen (tetrahedron adds the chain reaction).
Accelerants (petrol, kerosene) are recovered from debris by headspace sampling and identified by GC.
Low explosives deflagrate (black powder); high explosives detonate (TNT, RDX, PETN).
outcomes: Locate the seat of fire and identify accelerants

topics.title: Chromatography and spectroscopy in forensics
topics.summary: TLC, GC, HPLC, UV-Vis, IR and mass spectrometry.
notes: Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front.
GC separates volatile compounds; HPLC non-volatile ones; MS identifies compounds by mass-to-charge ratio.
IR spectroscopy identifies functional groups; UV-Vis follows Beer–Lambert's law A = εcl.
outcomes: Choose an instrument for an analysis

courses.title: Forensic Biology and Serology, BSc Semester 5
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (SEP 2024 (BU scheme to confirm), 2026-27)

topics.title: Hair and fibres
topics.summary: Microscopic examination of hair and fibres.
notes: Human hair has a medullary index usually below 1/3; animal hair above 1/2.
Scale patterns (imbricate in humans) and medulla type distinguish species.
Fibres are natural (cotton, wool, silk) or synthetic (nylon, polyester); compared by microscopy, birefringence and dye.

topics.title: Blood: identification and grouping
topics.summary: Presumptive and confirmatory tests for blood and ABO grouping.
notes: Presumptive tests: phenolphthalein (Kastle–Meyer), benzidine, luminol (chemiluminescence).
Confirmatory: Teichmann (haemin crystals), Takayama (haemochromogen crystals).
Precipitin test decides human or animal origin.
ABO grouping by agglutination with anti-A and anti-B; Rh with anti-D.
outcomes: Identify blood stains with presumptive and confirmatory tests

lesson.hook: A brown stain on a shirt: blood, rust or tea? How would you find out without destroying it?

questions.q: Which test detects blood by chemiluminescence?
Blood agglutinates with anti-A but not anti-B. Group?

topics.title: Bloodstain pattern analysis
topics.summary: Types of bloodstains and determining the point of origin.
notes: Passive stains (drops, flows), transfer stains (smears, swipes) and projected stains (spatter, arterial).
Angle of impact: sin θ = width ÷ length of the stain.
Area of convergence (2-D) and point of origin (3-D) are found from several stains.

topics.title: Semen and saliva
topics.summary: Identifying semen, saliva and other fluids.
notes: Acid phosphatase test is presumptive for semen; PSA (p30) and spermatozoa are confirmatory.
Alternate light sources show fluids by fluorescence.
Salivary amylase (starch–iodine test) indicates saliva.
outcomes: Explain the use of alternate light sources

resources.title: Effect of temperature and pH on salivary amylase

topics.title: DNA typing
topics.summary: DNA structure, extraction, PCR and STR profiling.
notes: STRs are short tandem repeats of 2–6 bases; forensic profiles type 15–20+ STR loci and amelogenin (sex).
Workflow: extraction, quantification, PCR amplification, capillary electrophoresis, interpretation.
Mitochondrial DNA (maternal) and Y-STRs (paternal) help with degraded samples and male lineages.
A match with a reference sample is reported with its random match probability; clear differences at typed loci exclude the reference as the source.

courses.title: Forensic Medicine and Anthropology, BSc Semester 5
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (SEP 2024 (BU scheme to confirm), 2026-27)

topics.title: Signs of death and time since death
topics.summary: Death, early and late post-mortem changes.
notes: Early changes: algor mortis (cooling, roughly 1 °C per hour early on), livor mortis (hypostasis, fixed in about 6–8 hours), rigor mortis (begins 2–6 hours, full by about 12, passes by 24–36 hours).
Late changes: decomposition, adipocere, mummification.
Entomology (insect succession) helps estimate time since death in later stages.
outcomes: Estimate time since death from post-mortem changes
Explain factors affecting cooling and rigor

topics.title: Mechanical injuries
topics.summary: Abrasions, contusions, lacerations, incised and stab wounds.
notes: Abrasion: loss of superficial skin; contusion: bruise from ruptured vessels; laceration: tear from blunt force.
Incised wounds are longer than deep with clean edges; stab wounds are deeper than long.
Defence wounds on hands and forearms suggest the victim resisted.
outcomes: Distinguish suicidal, homicidal and accidental wounds

topics.title: Asphyxial deaths
topics.summary: Hanging, strangulation, drowning and smothering.
notes: Hanging: ligature mark oblique, above the thyroid, incomplete; ligature strangulation: horizontal, below the thyroid, complete.
Drowning signs: froth at mouth and nostrils, water in the stomach, diatoms in bone marrow.
Petechial haemorrhages are seen in many asphyxial deaths.

topics.title: Identification from skeletal and dental remains
topics.summary: Estimating sex, age and stature from bones and teeth.
notes: Sex: pelvis (wider sub-pubic angle in females) and skull features.
Age: epiphyseal fusion and ossification centres in the young; dental eruption in children.
Stature from long bones (e.g. femur) using regression formulae.
Bite marks and dental records aid identification.
outcomes: Estimate sex and age from skeletal remains

courses.title: Digital and Cyber Forensics, BSc Semester 6
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (SEP 2024 (BU scheme to confirm), 2026-27)

topics.title: Cyber crimes and the law
topics.summary: Types of cyber crime and provisions of the IT Act.
notes: Cyber crimes: hacking, phishing, identity theft, cyberstalking, ransomware, online financial fraud, child sexual abuse material.
IT Act, 2000 sections 43 (civil liability), 66 (computer offences), 66C (identity theft), 66D (cheating by impersonation), 67 (obscene material).
Electronic records are admissible under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam with a certificate (section 63).

topics.title: Acquisition and preservation
topics.summary: Seizing devices, forensic imaging and hashing.
notes: Order of volatility: registers and cache, RAM, network state, disk, backups.
A forensic image is a bit-by-bit copy made through a write blocker.
Hash values (MD5, SHA-256) verify that the image matches the original.

topics.title: File systems and artefacts
topics.summary: Recovering deleted files and analysing system artefacts.
notes: Deleted files often remain in unallocated space until overwritten; file carving uses headers and footers.
Artefacts: browser history, registry, logs, metadata (EXIF), timestamps (MAC times).
Tools: Autopsy/Sleuth Kit, FTK, EnCase.

topics.title: Mobile and network evidence
topics.summary: Extracting data from phones and analysing network traffic.
notes: Extraction levels: manual, logical, file system, physical (chip-off).
Call detail records and tower dumps place a phone in time and space.
Packet captures (Wireshark) and logs reconstruct network events.

courses.title: Forensic Psychology and Victimology, BSc Semester 6
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (SEP 2024 (BU scheme to confirm), 2026-27)

topics.title: Scope and methods
topics.summary: Psychology applied to law: assessment, testimony and offender profiling.
notes: Forensic psychologists assess competence, risk and mental state, and assist investigations.
Offender profiling infers characteristics from crime scene behaviour (organised vs disorganised).
Psychological autopsy reconstructs a deceased person's state of mind.
outcomes: Describe the work of forensic psychologists

topics.title: Polygraph, narco-analysis and brain mapping
topics.summary: Deception detection techniques and their legal status.
notes: The polygraph records heart rate, blood pressure, respiration and skin conductance.
Selvi v State of Karnataka (2010): narco-analysis, polygraph and BEAP cannot be done without consent, and results are not admissible as such.
Information discovered as a result of a voluntary test may be admitted.
outcomes: State the legal position after Selvi

topics.title: Memory and interviewing
topics.summary: Reliability of eyewitnesses and the cognitive interview.
notes: Memory is reconstructive; leading questions can alter recall (Loftus).
Factors: stress, weapon focus, cross-race effect, delay.
The cognitive interview improves recall without leading.

topics.title: Victims and justice
topics.summary: Victim typologies, victim rights and compensation.
notes: Mendelsohn's typology ranges from completely innocent to most guilty victims.
Secondary victimisation is further harm from the justice process.
Victim compensation schemes operate under BNSS section 396.

courses.title: Chemistry: Atomic Structure and Analytical Chemistry, BSc Semester 1

topics.title: Quantum model of the atom
topics.summary: Quantum numbers, orbitals and electronic configuration.
notes: Quantum numbers: n (shell), l (subshell, 0 to n − 1), mₗ (−l to +l), mₛ (±½).
Aufbau principle (n + l rule), Pauli exclusion principle, Hund's rule.
Half-filled and fully filled subshells are extra stable (Cr: 3d⁵4s¹, Cu: 3d¹⁰4s¹).
de Broglie wavelength λ = h ÷ mv; Heisenberg: Δx·Δp ≥ h ÷ 4π.

topics.title: Periodic trends
topics.summary: Atomic radius, ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity.
notes: Atomic radius decreases across a period and increases down a group.
Ionisation energy increases across a period (with exceptions at groups 13 and 16).
Electronegativity (Pauling scale) is highest for fluorine (4.0).
Effective nuclear charge Z* = Z − S (Slater's rules).
outcomes: Compute effective nuclear charge with Slater's rules

topics.title: Titrimetric analysis
topics.summary: Concentration terms, standard solutions and acid–base titrations.
notes: Molarity = moles of solute ÷ litres of solution; normality = gram equivalents ÷ litres.
N₁V₁ = N₂V₂ at the equivalence point.
Primary standards (oxalic acid, sodium carbonate) are pure and stable; NaOH must be standardised.
Indicators: phenolphthalein (pH 8.2–10), methyl orange (3.1–4.4).

resources.title: Strength of hydrochloric acid by titration

lesson.hook: How can a few drops of an indicator tell you exactly how much acid is in a flask?
lesson.example: 20 mL of 0.1 N oxalic acid needs 25 mL NaOH. N(NaOH) = 0.1 × 20 ÷ 25 = 0.08 N.

questions.q: Why is NaOH not a primary standard?
questions.a: It absorbs moisture and CO₂ from the air, so its mass is not reliable.

topics.title: Redox titrations
topics.summary: Oxidising and reducing agents and permanganometry.
notes: KMnO₄ is a self-indicator: in acid it is reduced from Mn(VII) to Mn²⁺ (colourless).
Equivalent weight of KMnO₄ in acid medium = molar mass ÷ 5.
Oxalic acid titration is carried out warm (60–70 °C) in dilute H₂SO₄.

topics.title: Errors in chemical analysis
topics.summary: Accuracy, precision, errors and significant figures.
notes: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated measurements.
Determinate (systematic) errors can be corrected; indeterminate (random) errors cannot.
Report results with appropriate significant figures; standard deviation measures precision.
outcomes: Report results with correct significant figures

courses.title: Chemistry: Basic Organic Chemistry, BSc Semester 2

topics.title: Hybridisation and electronic effects
topics.summary: Hybridisation, inductive, resonance and hyperconjugation effects.
notes: sp³ (109.5°, tetrahedral), sp² (120°, trigonal), sp (180°, linear).
Inductive effect is permanent polarisation through σ bonds; −I groups (NO₂, Cl) withdraw electrons.
Resonance delocalises π electrons; hyperconjugation explains stability of alkyl-substituted carbocations.
Carbocation stability: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl.

topics.title: Substitution and elimination
topics.summary: SN1, SN2, E1 and E2 mechanisms.
notes: SN2: one step, backside attack, inversion of configuration, rate = k[RX][Nu]; favoured for 1° substrates.
SN1: carbocation intermediate, racemisation, rate = k[RX]; favoured for 3° substrates and polar protic solvents.
E2 needs an anti-periplanar H; Zaitsev's rule gives the more substituted alkene.

lesson.hook: Why does tert-butyl bromide react fast in water but slowly with a strong nucleophile in acetone?

questions.q: What happens to configuration in an SN2 reaction?
Which substrate reacts fastest by SN1: 1°, 2° or 3°?
questions.a: 3°, because it forms the most stable carbocation.

topics.title: Isomerism and chirality
topics.summary: Structural and stereoisomerism, R/S and E/Z nomenclature.
notes: A chiral carbon has four different groups; enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images.
CIP priority by atomic number assigns R (clockwise) or S (anticlockwise) with the lowest priority away.
Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images; meso compounds are achiral despite chiral centres.
E/Z for alkenes uses CIP priorities on each carbon.
outcomes: Identify enantiomers, diastereomers and meso forms

topics.title: Alkanes, alkenes and arenes
topics.summary: Preparation and reactions of hydrocarbons and aromaticity.
notes: Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition; Markovnikov's rule: H adds to the carbon with more H atoms.
Peroxide effect (anti-Markovnikov) applies to HBr only.
Hückel's rule: planar cyclic conjugated systems with (4n + 2) π electrons are aromatic.
Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution (nitration, halogenation, sulphonation, Friedel–Crafts).
outcomes: Predict addition products using Markovnikov's rule

courses.title: Chemistry: Physical Chemistry I, BSc Semester 3

topics.title: Real gases
topics.summary: Kinetic theory, deviations from ideal behaviour and the van der Waals equation.
notes: Ideal gas: PV = nRT; kinetic energy per mole = (3/2)RT.
van der Waals: (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT; a corrects attraction, b volume.
Compressibility factor Z = PV ÷ nRT; Z = 1 for an ideal gas.
outcomes: Use the van der Waals equation

topics.title: First and second laws
topics.summary: Internal energy, enthalpy, entropy and free energy.
notes: First law: ΔU = q + w.
ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT.
Gibbs free energy ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; a process is spontaneous at constant T and P if ΔG < 0.
Hess's law: enthalpy change is independent of path.

topics.title: Rate laws and order
topics.summary: Rate, order, molecularity, integrated rate laws and Arrhenius equation.
notes: First-order: k = (2.303/t) log([A]₀/[A]); half-life t½ = 0.693 ÷ k, independent of concentration.
Zero-order: [A] = [A]₀ − kt.
Arrhenius: k = A e^(−Ea/RT); log(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/2.303R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂).
outcomes: Determine order and rate constants from data

resources.title: Kinetics of acid hydrolysis of methyl acetate
Rate of reaction: sodium thiosulphate and acid

lesson.example:
A first-order reaction has k = 0.0693 min⁻¹. t½ = 0.693 ÷ 0.0693 = 10 min.
After 30 min (3 half-lives), 1/8 of the reactant remains.

topics.title: Viscosity, surface tension and colligative properties
topics.summary: Properties of liquids and colligative properties of solutions.
notes: Ostwald viscometer: η₁/η₂ = d₁t₁ ÷ d₂t₂.
Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles: relative lowering of vapour pressure, ΔTb = Kb m, ΔTf = Kf m, osmotic pressure π = CRT.
van't Hoff factor i corrects for dissociation or association.
outcomes: Compute molar mass from colligative data

resources.title: Viscosity of liquids with an Ostwald viscometer

courses.title: Chemistry: Coordination and Inorganic Chemistry, BSc Semester 4

topics.title: Werner's theory and nomenclature
topics.summary: Coordination number, ligands, IUPAC names and isomerism.
notes: Werner: primary valency (oxidation state, ionisable) and secondary valency (coordination number, directional).
Ligands: monodentate (NH₃, Cl⁻), bidentate (en, ox²⁻), polydentate (EDTA⁴⁻, hexadentate); chelates are extra stable.
Isomerism: ionisation, linkage, geometrical (cis/trans), optical.
outcomes: Name coordination compounds by IUPAC rules

topics.title: Bonding in complexes
topics.summary: Valence bond theory and crystal field theory.
notes: Octahedral crystal field splits d orbitals into t₂g (lower) and e_g (higher) by Δo.
Strong-field ligands (CN⁻, CO) give low-spin complexes; weak-field (F⁻, H₂O) high-spin (spectrochemical series).
Magnetic moment μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM for n unpaired electrons.

topics.title: s- and p-block compounds
topics.summary: Hydrides, oxides, halides and important compounds.
notes: Diagonal relationship: Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si.
Boranes have electron-deficient three-centre two-electron bonds (diborane).
Silicates are built from SiO₄ tetrahedra; silicones have Si–O–Si chains with organic groups.
outcomes: Explain anomalous properties of first elements
Describe the structure of diborane and silicates

topics.title: Semi-micro qualitative analysis
topics.summary: Group separation of cations and tests for anions.
notes: Cation groups by precipitating reagent: I HCl, II H₂S in acid, III NH₄OH/NH₄Cl, IV H₂S in ammoniacal medium, V (NH₄)₂CO₃, VI none.
Common ion effect controls precipitation in groups II and IV.
Flame colours: Na golden yellow, K lilac, Ca brick red, Sr crimson, Ba apple green, Cu blue-green.

topics.title: Crystal structures
topics.summary: Unit cells, packing and defects.
notes: Cubic cells: simple (1 atom per cell), bcc (2), fcc (4).
Packing efficiency: sc 52.4%, bcc 68%, fcc/hcp 74%.
Defects: Schottky (cation–anion vacancy pair, lowers density) and Frenkel (ion displaced to interstitial site).
outcomes: Compute atoms per unit cell and density

courses.title: Chemistry: Spectroscopy and Electrochemistry, BSc Semester 5
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (SEP 2024 (BU scheme to confirm), 2026-27)

topics.title: UV-Visible and IR spectroscopy
topics.summary: Electronic transitions, Beer–Lambert law and IR functional group frequencies.
notes: Beer–Lambert law: A = εcl.
UV-Vis transitions: σ→σ*, n→σ*, π→π*, n→π*; conjugation shifts λmax to longer wavelength.
IR: O–H about 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ (broad), C=O about 1700 cm⁻¹, C≡N about 2250 cm⁻¹.
outcomes: Identify functional groups from IR spectra

topics.title: NMR and mass spectrometry
topics.summary: Chemical shift, splitting and molecular ion.
notes: ¹H NMR chemical shift (ppm from TMS) depends on electronic environment; aldehyde H ≈ 9–10 ppm.
n + 1 rule: a proton with n equivalent neighbours splits into n + 1 peaks.
In MS, the molecular ion peak gives the molar mass; the base peak is the most intense.
outcomes: Find molar mass from a mass spectrum

topics.title: Conductance
topics.summary: Conductivity, molar conductivity and Kohlrausch's law.
notes: Molar conductivity Λm = κ × 1000 ÷ C.
Strong electrolytes: Λm = Λ°m − A√C; weak electrolytes: degree of dissociation α = Λm ÷ Λ°m.
Kohlrausch's law: Λ°m = ν₊λ°₊ + ν₋λ°₋.
outcomes: Compute molar conductivity and degree of dissociation

resources.title: Conductometric titration of acids with NaOH

topics.title: Electrochemical cells
topics.summary: EMF, Nernst equation and pH measurement.
notes: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode.
Nernst equation: E = E° − (0.0591/n) log Q at 298 K.
ΔG° = −nFE°.
pH is measured with a glass electrode; pH-metric titration finds the equivalence point from the steepest rise.
outcomes: Compute cell EMF with the Nernst equation

courses.title: Chemistry: Polymers, Green and Industrial Chemistry, BSc Semester 6
courses.source: kinetix-curriculum-team from public BU syllabus (SEP 2024 (BU scheme to confirm), 2026-27)

topics.title: Polymerisation and polymers
topics.summary: Addition and condensation polymers and their properties.
notes: Addition (chain-growth) polymers: polythene, PVC, polystyrene; condensation (step-growth): nylon-6,6, polyester, Bakelite.
Thermoplastics soften on heating; thermosets do not.
Number-average molar mass Mn = ΣNᵢMᵢ ÷ ΣNᵢ; weight-average Mw = ΣNᵢMᵢ² ÷ ΣNᵢMᵢ.

topics.title: Principles of green chemistry
topics.summary: The twelve principles and atom economy.
notes: Twelve principles include waste prevention, atom economy, safer solvents and energy efficiency.
Atom economy = molar mass of desired product ÷ total molar mass of reactants × 100.
Catalysis and renewable feedstocks reduce environmental impact.

topics.title: Chromatography and extraction
topics.summary: Paper, TLC, column chromatography and solvent extraction.
notes: Separation depends on partition between stationary and mobile phases.

topics.summary: Fertilisers, cement, water treatment and pollution.
notes: Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (iron catalyst, about 200 atm, 700 K).
Water hardness: temporary (bicarbonates, removed by boiling) and permanent (chlorides, sulphates); EDTA titration measures it.
BOD and COD measure organic pollution of water.
